summary: Gives extra security considerations for OAuth 2.0 based on a broad threat model of the protocol. It describes attacks against clients, authorization servers and tokens, and suggests countermeasures. It is informational and complements the OAuth 2.0 specification.

eli5.summary: A list of the ways a thief might trick a building's key-card system, with advice on locks and habits that stop each trick.

subtitle: A catalog of the ways OAuth 2.0 can be attacked, each paired with the countermeasures that blunt it.

tldr.problem: The OAuth 2.0 specification gives limited security guidance, and implementers need to know which attacks to expect against clients, authorization servers, tokens and protected resources.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC states its attack and architecture assumptions, describes the security features built into OAuth, then walks through threats grouped by component and flow, each with impact and countermeasures that point to a detailed section on defenses.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational companion to the OAuth 2.0 specification. It does not rate the risk of any threat, and it has been updated by RFC 9700.

today: RFC 6819 is Informational and has been updated by RFC 9700. It was not obsoleted, and it remains a companion to the OAuth 2.0 framework in RFC 6749.

sections.title: Scope and Assumptions
sections.content:
RFC 6819 gives security considerations for OAuth beyond those in the core specification (RFC 6749), based on a comprehensive threat model. It describes the assumptions made, the security features built into OAuth, and the threats with their countermeasures. Threats are laid out along the protocol structure so a team can look up, for example, every threat for one grant type or every threat for the resource server.

The document considers only clients bound to a particular deployment, with static, well-known resource server URLs and token scopes. It treats as out of scope the communication between authorization server and resource server, token formats, how the server authenticates the user (except for the password grant), and clients not tied to one deployment. It deliberately does not assess the probability or risk of a threat, because that depends on the application.

The attacker is assumed to have full access to the network between client and authorization server and between client and resource server, to have unlimited resources, and to be able to make two of the three parties collude against the third. The attacker is not assumed to see traffic between the authorization server and the resource server.
sections.eli5: Before listing the tricks, the document says what it assumes: the bad guy can listen to the mail between you and the shops, has lots of time, and might even be working with one of the shops.

sections.title: Built-in Security Features
sections.content:
OAuth makes heavy use of tokens, and a token's information can be held in two ways. A handle is a reference to data stored at the authorization server; it makes revocation simple, but the resource server must talk to the issuer to validate it. An assertion is a parseable, usually signed token that a resource server can validate alone, which scales better but makes revocation harder. Tokens are used either as bearer tokens, which any holder can use, so communication must be protected, or as proof tokens, where each use requires the client to show it is the rightful user.

Other built-in features limit damage. A scope restricts what a token can do, and expires_in lets the server limit an access token's lifetime. Access tokens are short-lived (minutes or hours) and are renewed with a long-lasting refresh token that only travels between client and authorization server, so access can be revoked passively when the current access token expires. The authorization code is sent to the redirect URI instead of a token, and is exchanged over a more secure direct connection where the client can be authenticated.

The redirect URI is checked when the code is exchanged, which helps detect malicious clients and phishing. The state parameter links requests and callbacks to prevent cross-site request forgery. The client identifier lets the server tie requests to one originator, and the RFC ranks several client identity models by how much can be validated and how widely revoking one affects deployments.
sections.eli5: OAuth gives out short-lived visitor passes, keeps a separate long-term pass locked away, and checks the return address on every delivery, so a stolen pass is less useful.

sections.title: Threats Against Clients and Endpoints
sections.content:
Section 4 groups threats by component. For clients, an attacker may extract a client secret from source code or a binary, even an obfuscated one, or steal refresh tokens and access tokens from a web server or a native device by reading storage, stealing or cloning the device. A malicious app may phish passwords by presenting its own or an embedded browser instead of the system browser. Open redirectors on a client are dangerous when the server lets the client register only part of its redirect URI.

At the authorization endpoint, threats include password phishing by a counterfeit authorization server (OAuth does not authenticate the server by itself), a user granting too much scope, a malicious client reusing an earlier authorization that the server approves automatically, and abuse of the server as an open redirector.

At the token endpoint, threats include eavesdropping access tokens or client credentials in transit, stealing tokens or client secrets from the authorization server database, and online guessing of client secrets. Each threat in the RFC lists its impact and countermeasures, such as TLS, limited scope, short lifetimes, strong client authentication and standard database protections.
sections.eli5: A thief can copy the key from a careless app, pretend to be the front desk, or trick you into handing over too many keys. Each trick has a matching lock.

sections.title: Threats in Each Grant Flow
sections.content:
For the authorization code flow, the RFC covers leaking codes through referrer headers, request logs, open redirectors and browser history. It also covers a cross-site request forgery (CSRF) attack on the redirect URI, where an attacker obtains a code for their own resources, aborts the redirect on their device and tricks the victim into completing it, so the victim's client session ends up tied to the attacker's resources. The countermeasure is to use the state parameter to bind the request to the user agent session. Clickjacking, where a hidden frame sits under dummy buttons, is countered by the X-FRAME-OPTIONS header on newer browsers.

In the implicit grant, the access token is returned as a URI fragment, which user agents do not send to servers, so it cannot leak through referrer headers. It can still leak in transport or in browser history, and the RFC advises short expiry, reduced scope and non-cacheable responses.

The resource owner password credentials grant carries the highest warning. It keeps the user id and password anti-pattern, the user does not control the authorization step, scope limits do not really apply, and revocation is bypassed. The RFC says to minimize its use except for migration and to limit it to cases where client and authorizing service are from the same organization.
sections.eli5: Some ways of getting a pass are safer than others. The riskiest is handing your password straight to the app, so the document says to avoid it unless the app and the service belong to the same company.

sections.title: Countermeasures
sections.content:
Section 5 collects the defenses that the threats refer to. Confidentiality of requests comes first: OAuth verifies request integrity but gives no guarantee of confidentiality, so TLS is the main answer, and the document assumes end-to-end TLS between protocol entities.

For tokens, the RFC recommends limiting scope, choosing an expiration that fits the risk (a few minutes for payments, hours for read access to contacts), using short lifetimes, and limiting use to a single time or a few times. If an authorization code is redeemed more than once, the server may revoke the tokens granted from it. Tokens can be bound to a resource server (an audience), bound to a client id, signed, encrypted, and carried in a standard assertion format.

For refresh tokens, rotation changes the value on every refresh request so a stolen token used in parallel is detected; since the server cannot tell attacker from client, it then revokes the valid token and its authorization. The RFC notes this can cause problems in clustered deployments. Other defenses include validating the client id on every refresh, device identification, and revocation.

The closing section warns that OAuth puts the end user inside the security model: users often cannot judge what they approve, and malicious user-installed apps can steal credentials, over-request authorization or automate approvals. The RFC says no solution is offered because none is known.
sections.eli5: The fixes are simple habits: seal the envelope, use passes that expire fast, change the spare key every time it is used, and tell people clearly what they are agreeing to.
